teaser: A boy who never bowed to an idol, struck down at dawn while calling people to prayer.
quran_mention: He is not named in the Qur'an. The ayah he quoted about the man who assassinated him was «وَلَا تَعْتَدُوا إِنَّ اللَّهَ لَا يُحِبُّ الْمُعْتَدِينَ» — 'and do not transgress; Allah does not love the transgressors.' (2:190)

layers.title: Who He Was
layers.subtitle: A patched waist-wrapper and a whip in the market
layers.content:
Ali ibn Abi Talib ibn Abd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim. His kunya was Abu al-Hasan. His mother was Fatima bint Asad ibn Hashim, so both his parents were of the Prophet's own clan.

The men who saw him agree on the beard. ash-Sha'bi: 'He had a large beard which filled all that was between his shoulders.' It went white and he mostly left it undyed. He was balding, taller than middling, heavy through the shoulders and arms and thin in the lower legs, with kohl on his eyes. In the market of Kufa the traders would call after him, 'A full belly.' He answered: 'The top of it is knowledge and the bottom is food.'

He walked those markets himself with a small whip, telling people to fear Allah and trade well. Give full weight and measure. Do not blow on the meat to plump it up.

Someone once asked him why the amir al-mu'minin was wearing a patched wrapper. 'The heart is humbled, and the believer is ransomed by it.' He bought a plain shirt for four dirhams and made the tailor cut the sleeves level with his fingertips, and then said out loud: 'Praise be to Allah, who clothed Ali ibn Abi Talib.'
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley

layers.title: The Conversion
layers.subtitle: He was too young to have ever worshipped an idol
layers.content:
Ibn Sa'd sets out the disagreement instead of hiding it, and it is worth hearing in his own words: 'Our companions agree that the first of the people of the qibla to respond to the Messenger of Allah was Khadijah bint Khuwaylid. Then we disagree about which of three people first became Muslim: Abu Bakr, Ali, or Zayd ibn Harithah.'

Zayd ibn Arqam said Ali was the first to accept Islam with the Prophet ﷺ, and another narrator adds, 'He was the first to pray.' Mujahid says he was ten years old when he prayed. Others say nine. al-Hasan ibn Zayd, his own descendant, reports it was said he was younger still, and notes the consequence: he never worshipped idols, because he was too young to have started.

That is the strange shape of his entry. The other early Muslims had something to renounce — wealth, standing, a family religion. Ali had almost nothing yet to give up. What Islam cost him was not a past. It was every year of the life ahead of him, beginning with a boyhood spent inside a household under siege by its own tribe.

He was raised in the Prophet's house. He grew up standing next to the prayer before there was a community to pray with.
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley (reports of Zayd ibn Arqam, Mujahid, Ibn Abbas)

layers.title: With the Prophet ﷺ
layers.subtitle: The banner in every battle, and the dust off his heels
layers.content:
When the Prophet ﷺ left for Madinah, Ali stayed behind on purpose. People had left deposits with the Prophet ﷺ because he was called the Trustworthy, and someone had to give them back. 'I stayed for three days, and I showed myself and did not conceal myself for a single day.' Then he walked out after him and caught him still at Quba.

When the brotherhood pairings were made, the Prophet ﷺ put his hand on Ali's shoulder and said, 'You are my brother.' Qatada reports that Ali carried the Prophet's banner at Badr and in every battle; another narrator says the standard travelled in other hands on the march, but the moment there was fighting, Ali took it. He held his ground at Uhud when others fell back.

Only one campaign went without him. Left in Madinah over the families during Tabuk, he heard people saying he had been left behind because the Prophet ﷺ had gone cold on him. He rode out after the army to ask. The Prophet ﷺ laughed and said: 'Are you not content to be in relation to me as Harun was to Musa, except that there will be no Prophet after me?' Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab's narrator remembered the ending best — Ali turned and went back so fast you could see the dust off his feet.
layers.hadith_ref: The Prophet ﷺ said to Ali at Tabuk: 'Are you not content to be in relation to me as Harun was to Musa, except that there will be no Prophet after me?' — narrated by Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Ibn Sa'd Tabaqat Vol. III
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley

layers.title: The Trial
layers.subtitle: Four years in which believers faced believers
layers.content:
He was given allegiance in Madinah the day after Uthman was killed — by Talha, az-Zubayr, Sa'id ibn Zayd, Ammar ibn Yasir, Usama, Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, Zayd ibn Thabit and the companions who were there. On the day of the killing itself, sitting in a black turban, he said only: 'Loss to you for the rest of time.'

What followed is the hardest stretch of this history to narrate. Muslims fought Muslims at the Camel, and Talha and az-Zubayr were among the dead. They fought again at Siffin, where Ammar ibn Yasir and Khuzayma ibn Thabit were killed on Ali's side. When copies of the Qur'an were raised in the Syrian ranks and an arbitration was agreed, a faction of his own army broke away over it, declaring that judgement belongs to Allah alone, and he ended up fighting them too at Nahrawan.

Companions of the Prophet ﷺ stood on more than one side of those fields. The ummah has never reached one verdict on them, and this is not the place where one gets handed down. Ibn Sa'd records Ali's own prayer from those years, which is the most honest summary of them anyone has left us: 'O Allah, I am weary of them and they are weary of me. So mercy to them from me, and show mercy to me from them.'
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley

layers.title: The Legacy
layers.subtitle: Struck at dawn, and still setting limits on revenge
layers.content:
He had been saying for a while that his beard would be dyed with blood from his head. People pressed him for the name so they could destroy the man's family. He refused: 'By Allah, then you would kill by me other than my killer.'

Before dawn on the night it happened he told al-Hasan he had seen the Prophet ﷺ in a dream and complained to him of the burdens and quarrels of his community. Then the mu'adhdhin came. Ali went out with his whip calling, 'People, the prayer, the prayer,' as he did every morning. Two swords came at him from the dark and a voice cried that judgement belongs to Allah, not to him. One blow reached his brain.

His instruction about the captive is his most unlikely legacy. Feed him well. Give him a soft bed. 'If I live, I am more entitled to his blood, by either pardon or retaliation. If I die, then kill him for killing me. Do not go beyond that. Allah does not love those who transgress.' He also wrote to his eldest son: no mutilation.

He lived through the day and died that night, in Ramadan 40 AH, at sixty-three. His caliphate had lasted four years and nine months. His sons washed him. He left seven hundred dirhams, saved to buy a servant.
layers.quran_ref: Quran 2:190 — 'and do not transgress; Allah does not love the transgressors'
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley (narrations of al-Hasan ibn Ali and Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya)

quiz.prompt: Why did Ali stay behind in Makkah for three days after the Prophet ﷺ left on the Hijra?

options.text: To lead the remaining Muslims in prayer
To return the deposits people had entrusted to the Prophet ﷺ
To mislead Quraysh about the direction taken
To settle a debt owed by Abu Talib

quiz.citation: Narrated by Ubaydullah ibn Abi Rafi from Ali — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: People had left goods with the Prophet ﷺ because he was called the Trustworthy. Ali said he stayed three days and never once hid himself — the goods came back to their owners in daylight.

quiz.prompt: What did Ibn Sa'd report that his teachers agreed on regarding who first accepted Islam?

options.text: That it was Ali, without dispute
That it was Abu Bakr, without dispute
That Khadijah was first, and they differed over Abu Bakr, Ali and Zayd ibn Harithah after her
That the order was never recorded at all

quiz.citation: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: Ibn Sa'd states the agreement and the disagreement in the same breath. It is a useful habit: what is settled, and what remains open, kept clearly apart.

quiz.prompt: What did the Prophet ﷺ say to Ali when he rode out to Tabuk to ask why he had been left behind?

options.text: 'Return, for Madinah needs you more than I do'
'Are you not content to be in relation to me as Harun was to Musa, except that there will be no Prophet after me?'
'You will be tested more than any of them'
'Bring the banner and march at the front'

quiz.citation: Narrated by Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: Ali had come because people were whispering that he was out of favour. He went home so quickly that the narrator remembered the dust rising off his heels.

quiz.prompt: What answer did Ali give when people demanded he name his would-be killer so they could act first?

options.text: He named him and forbade them to touch him
'By Allah, then you would kill by me other than my killer'
He said the man had already repented
He said no man could harm him before his term came

quiz.citation: Narrated by Abdullah ibn Saba from Ali — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: They had offered to destroy the man's family. He refused to let his own killing become the cause of other killings — a limit he set while the wound was still ahead of him.

quiz.prompt: How much wealth did Ali leave behind at his death?

options.text: Nothing at all
Seven hundred dirhams, set aside to buy a servant
The estate at Fadak
Forty thousand dirhams, distributed to the poor of Kufa

quiz.citation: The khutba of al-Hasan ibn Ali after his father's death — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: He had governed from Egypt to Persia. What was in the house was seven hundred dirhams and a plan to buy help for the household.

quiz.prompt: Ali wore a patched wrapper and said the heart is humbled by it. What is your relationship with looking less well-off than you are?

options.text: I dress to be taken seriously and I know it
I do not think about it much either way
I would find it genuinely hard to be seen as shabby
I prefer plain, but partly because that is also a statement

quiz.citation: Reflection on the reports of Ali's dress, Ibn Sa'd Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: He was the head of state when he was seen in it. Notice that he gave a reason about his own heart, not about anyone watching.

quiz.prompt: He walked back from Tabuk satisfied by a single sentence, after a rumour had wounded him. What settles you when you fear you have lost someone's regard?

options.text: One clear word from them and I am fine
I go quiet and never ask, so it stays unresolved
I need it said more than once before I believe it
I tell myself I do not need reassurance, which is not true

quiz.citation: Reflection on the Tabuk narration of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Ibn Sa'd Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: He did the unglamorous thing first: he went and asked directly instead of nursing the rumour. Most of the ache in this life comes from not asking.

quiz.prompt: Companions of the Prophet ﷺ stood on opposite sides at the Camel and Siffin. How do you hold that?

options.text: I would rather not think about it at all
I want a verdict and it unsettles me not to have one
I accept that righteous people can be on both sides of a disaster
I think restraint here is itself the lesson

quiz.citation: Reflection on the fitnah years as recorded in Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: The ummah has never settled on a single reading of those years, and the scholars who knew the most were often the most careful. There is no obligation on you to judge them.

quiz.prompt: Wounded, he ordered that his own assassin be fed well and given a soft bed, and that no one go beyond retaliation. Where would your instinct go?

options.text: Honestly, toward wanting more than fairness
Toward justice, but not toward kindness
I would want it handled by someone other than me
I like to think I would set the same limit and I am not sure

quiz.citation: Ali's instruction concerning Ibn Muljam — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: He quoted the Qur'an as he said it: 'Do not transgress. Allah does not love the transgressors' (2:190). Setting the ceiling on revenge is easier before you are the one bleeding.

quiz.prompt: Some people later made extravagant claims about Ali, and his own son al-Hasan publicly refused them. What does loving someone accurately require?

options.text: Refusing to add to them what they did not claim
Being willing to be the one who corrects the praise
Accepting they were human, which is the harder love
All of these, and none of them come naturally

quiz.citation: al-Hasan ibn Ali's response to those who claimed his father would return — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: Told that some claimed his father would come back before the Day of Rising, al-Hasan said they lied — and pointed out that his family had divided the estate and remarried the widows, which is what people do when a man has died.
